title: Postoperative SGLT2 restart after a fasting course

cues.phrase: should replace
cues.why: The task presupposes that the calendar instruction is wrong, eliminating the calendar option before clinical reasoning.

cues.phrase: the team has not reviewed that instruction since the vomiting began
cues.why: Flags an omitted review and explicitly connects the new symptom to the need to change the order.

cues.phrase: She still vomits after meals
cues.why: Paired with the sole option mentioning return of oral intake, ordinary symptom matching identifies the key; the alternatives do not compete on safe restart criteria.

cues.phrase: clinical stability and oral intake return
cues.why: The key is the only multi-criterion clinical recovery plan, against a date or single laboratory result.

fairness: Among the offered options, delayed resumption until recovery is the defensible answer; the stem does not supply a second substantive inference.
Importance: high; perioperative SGLT2 medication reconciliation is practical surgical care. Too easy for the requested PGY-2/3 challenge.

Realism: ongoing postoperative vomiting with hospital-team nutrition support needs a clearer care-transition setting. A medication-calendar question must not imply that reassessing the vomiting or possible metabolic illness is unnecessary.

Scope for this entire report: the supplied JSON has 39 variants, not 40, and no literal after blocks. Only equivalent visible clinical-case presentation, node exhibit/task and choice labels were scored; author rationales, metadata and titles were not used as answer cues. No current-update field was present. This offline editorial review neither verifies guideline currency nor grants clinical approval; all drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: Ask neutrally which medication instruction is appropriate now; remove the sentence announcing an unreviewed instruction.

Show the relevant intake, clinical trajectory and available metabolic observations, then compare three concrete restart/withhold plans with credible differing recovery criteria. Preserve necessary safety findings and have the clinician verify the restart conditions.
Clarify whether this is a current discharge review or a later clinic review of a past episode.

title: Respiratory recurrence after naloxone

cues.why: Directly selects the only option continuing respiratory care; a lay reader can reject ending observation.

cues.why: Advertises that discharge would ignore the subsequent deterioration already given.

cues.why: Limb strength is an obvious category mismatch for recurrent slow breathing and supplies no credible competing recovery plan.

fairness: The key is best, but 'respiratory support' is broad and the alternatives do not test a close management decision. Repeat reversal and cause-specific reassessment are not evaluated.
Importance: high; recurrent respiratory depression after reversal matters. This is basic safety recognition, too easy for a routine resident challenge.
Realism: review of a past recovery event is plausible, but the task does not say whether it asks what should have happened then or what to arrange now.
suggestions: Make the historical decision time explicit, or use a current monitored-recovery vignette.

Keep the red flags. Either seek acceptance as an easy safety item or compare concrete monitored airway/reversal plans after an initial response, with the medication and response chronology needed to distinguish them.
Remove discharge-at-an-earlier-time and limb-strength foils.

title: Ventilation despite a reassuring saturation display

cues.why: Against 'Repeat finger pulse oximetry', this makes the repeat option redundant rather than a plausible acquisition problem.

suggestions: Use a labelled constructed capnogram or serial ventilation observations and ask for a consequential interpretation or action.
Offer similarly scoped respiratory monitoring/response plans and retain supplemental oxygen as clinically necessary context.

title: Interpreting matched ventilator pressure changes

cues.why: Directly excludes 'Increased imposed inspiratory flow', leaving a binary elastic-versus-resistive choice.

fairness: The pressure changes support increased elastic load under the stated controlled passive conditions; the peak-minus-plateau difference is unchanged.
Importance: high ICU/ABSITE mechanics, but this is a single familiar classification without a subsequent decision. Too easy for the requested challenge.
Realism: a patient bringing paired ventilator mechanics to clinic solely for interpretation feels artificial. An explicitly retrospective ICU case conference would fit better.
The table is a usable numerical exhibit. No key length, grammar or convergence cue identified beyond the explicitly excluded flow distractor.
suggestions: Keep the acquisition controls because they make the comparison fair; replace the contradicted flow option with a credible mechanical alternative.
Add clinically relevant ventilator/patient observations that require distinguishing causes of increased elastic load and choosing a concrete next check.

title: Phosphate chronology before nutrition restart

cues.phrase: before any nutrition was administered
cues.why: Chronology alone disproves feeding causation; no medical knowledge is required.

cues.phrase: Before first nutrition
cues.why: Repeats the decisive chronology already supplied in the presentation.

cues.phrase: Nutrition delivered before sampling
cues.why: The 'None' entry repeats the same elimination a third time.

cues.phrase: restart monitoring can be omitted
cues.why: The otherwise matching baseline-depletion distractor appends an obviously incautious conclusion.

cues.phrase: a feeding-related change is unproven
cues.why: Only the key is calibrated to uncertainty; the other options claim proof or permission to omit monitoring.

fairness: The result precedes feeding, so attribution to that restart is unsupported. Low serum phosphate does not by itself prove the mechanism or extent of total-body depletion; prolonged poor intake makes depletion plausible, not established.
Importance: high for refeeding safety, but this item tests temporal logic and a label, with no nutrition decision. Too easy.
Realism: consultation before restarting nutrition is plausible; three repetitions of the timing and an obviously erroneous referral label are not needed.
suggestions: Use 'pre-existing hypophosphatemia' rather than asserting proven depletion from this result alone.
Replace the erroneous referral summary and redundant exhibit with a concise pre/post nutrition trajectory, then ask for a concrete monitoring or feeding-management decision.
Compare credible plans that all retain necessary monitoring; verify any added criteria with the clinician.

title: Perfusion before an early burn-feeding pathway

cues.why: Gives interpreted contraindications rather than observations to interpret, strongly selecting stabilization.

cues.phrase: A checklist cited early nutrition after extensive burns
cues.why: Sets up an obvious stale-checklist-versus-deteriorating-patient contrast.

fairness: Resuscitation before initiating feeding is the best offered priority in the described deterioration. The item should not teach that any circulatory support automatically precludes enteral nutrition.
Importance: high critical-care nutrition safety; too easy as written.
Realism: retrospective burn-center review can be educational but is not an actionable clinic nutrition decision. 'At that point' does correctly locate the historical choice.
suggestions: Show a concrete perfusion/support trajectory rather than 'worsening perfusion' and a preinterpreted ischemia concern.
Compare plausible timing/rate strategies in the same resuscitation context, retaining the clinical facts needed to distinguish active deterioration from stabilization.
Remove the parenteral-nutrition-as-resuscitation foil. Alternatively retain as an explicitly accepted safety-recognition item.

title: Nutrition delivery versus recovery of intestinal function

cues.phrase: oral trials still caused vomiting and the abdominal distension persisted
cues.why: Plainly contradicts the two options claiming established gastrointestinal recovery.

cues.phrase: proof that the ileus had resolved
cues.why: Overstated prior-note claim invites rejection without a close clinical alternative.

cues.why: Only the key acknowledges uncertainty; both distractors repeat the same overconfident recovery conclusion.

fairness: The key is the best supported conclusion, but stabilized weight is not a complete nutritional response assessment, and 'obstruction had been assessed' does not say what that assessment found.
Importance: nutrition versus bowel function is practical, but this narrow label distinction adds little beyond basic recognition. Too easy.
Realism: outpatient review after prolonged ileus is plausible; the historical/current status should be clearer if the result is meant to change care.
suggestions: Replace the erroneous note with an actual chronology of oral tolerance, output and relevant examination/imaging findings.
Ask for a specific next nutrition or diagnostic step, comparing credible alternatives rather than two copies of 'recovery established'.
State the relevant obstruction-assessment result if it affects the plan; do not equate assessment with exclusion.

title: Protein adequacy without calorie overfeeding

Realism: dietitian co-management is plausible, but an outside prescription calculation has no stated surgical indication. The care purpose should be concrete.
No numerical guideline range was verified in this offline review; clinician verification of the prescribed target is required.
suggestions: Provide the actual selected protein target if the task is implementation of a prescription, or explicitly ask the learner to select a target rather than claiming it is recorded.
Remove 'was being revised' and compare isocaloric formulations with credible protein amounts so the desired change is not announced.
Make the choice alter a real postoperative nutrition prescription while preserving the patient's noncritical dialysis status.

title: A collagen cofactor is not universal postoperative therapy

cues.phrase: uncomplicated healing incision and a varied diet

title: A new DVT changes anticoagulation purpose

cues.phrase: new proximal DVT
cues.why: The task supplies the diagnosis that the ultrasound observation could otherwise require the learner to infer.

cues.phrase: no active cancer, active bleeding or other documented anticoagulation contraindication
cues.why: The bleeding/contraindication exclusion removes the main reason to consider a different immediate path. Cancer and first-event negatives add no discrimination for this treatment-versus-prophylaxis task.

fairness: Therapeutic anticoagulation is the single best offered category for a new proximal DVT without a stated contraindication. Necessary safety exclusions should be preserved, not removed merely to make it harder.
Importance: very high, but this is basic diagnosis-to-treatment recognition, too easy for PGY-2/3 residents.

cues.phrase: conflates that plan with therapeutic bridging

cues.phrase: separately
cues.why: Preannounces that the two heparin decisions are independent.

fairness: The intended omission of routine therapeutic bridging while providing indicated surgical prophylaxis is plausible. The absent mechanical valve/recent stroke information is clinically useful, not something to remove automatically.

The matrix does not specify when bridging and prophylactic LMWH would be given. 'Add bridge and give prophylactic LMWH' could be read as concurrent duplicate anticoagulation or as separate phases, reducing distractor clarity.
Importance: high perioperative practice. Moderate for a PGY-2/3 learner unfamiliar with AF bridging guidance, but the second purported reasoning step is supplied.
Realism: preoperative clinic planning fits well. No patient-specific schedule, renal function or dose is given; this review does not claim an exact regimen is established.
suggestions: Replace the summarized prophylaxis eligibility with the concrete operation, mobility and relevant bleeding observations.
Remove 'conflates' and ask neutrally for the perioperative anticoagulation plan.

Retain the clinically necessary thromboembolic-risk history; verify any additional bridging-selection criteria.

title: Factor assays need not wait for a mixing-screen gate

cues.phrase: factor-specific assessment

cues.phrase: as the final factor-deficiency assessment
cues.why: Overclaims the role of a screening test and makes the third option a caricature rather than a credible sequence.

fairness: New bleeding with isolated prolonged aPTT makes prompt factor/inhibitor investigation plausible. However, the stem does not establish a clinically material delay from the mixing screen, local assay access, or an explicit acquired-inhibitor suspicion; a rapid sequential laboratory workflow may also be defensible.
'The laboratory has assessed specimen and anticoagulant interference' does not report the result of that assessment. It must not silently mean interference was excluded.

Difficulty is moderate from specialized workflow knowledge, not a supported two-step decision. No definite clinical inaccuracy is asserted; local workflow and guideline ranking need clinician verification.
suggestions: State the actual interference findings and availability/turnaround constraints if they determine whether waiting changes care.
Ask for the surgeon's concrete initial diagnostic/referral plan rather than what hematology 'should' do in an unspecified laboratory.
Compare plausible concurrently ordered or staged investigations and specify why delay matters; do not use a mixing test as a purported definitive factor diagnosis.

title: Purulence changes the purpose of wound care

title: Duct clearance does not remove the gallbladder source

title: Antibody results after a valid eradication test

cues.why: 'Valid' certifies the key from inside the option, while no competing option addresses a plausible limitation of the active test.

suggestions: Remove the option's self-certifying 'valid' and name the actual action, such as whether to retreat or obtain a specific repeat active test.

title: Continence history before irreversible sphincter division

cues.phrase: unassessed anal dilation
cues.why: 'Unassessed' is a rhetorical warning label that makes this competitor visibly careless.

fairness: Deferring irreversible sphincter division for continence-focused assessment is the best offered action. Baseline seepage and prior sphincter injury are necessary, consequential history and should remain.
Importance: high; avoiding worsened continence is important colorectal practice. Too easy because the task and distractors label the intended error.

Realism: this is a useful clinic referral-review scenario. 'Appropriate topical calcium-channel-blocker course' summarizes regimen adequacy without observations; if treatment failure drives the revised decision, name the actual regimen and course.
suggestions: Ask neutrally which plan is appropriate and remove 'absent from the referral' and 'unassessed'.
Compare concrete sphincter-preserving and sphincter-dividing strategies or specific assessment plans at the same stage.
Supply the treatment course and continence/examination findings needed to distinguish the closest options; obtain clinician confirmation of any procedural ranking.

title: Matching esophageal provocation to unexplained food symptoms

cues.phrase: during solid meals
cues.why: Matches the only solid-meal option directly, allowing a nonexpert to answer by matching the stimulus.

cues.phrase: remaining meal-associated question
cues.why: Repeats the match in the task itself.

cues.phrase: Rapid-swallow contractile-reserve sequence
cues.why: The distractor includes its different testing purpose, whereas the key repeats the presenting stimulus.

cues.phrase: separated water-swallow manometry series did not reproduce his symptoms or explain them
cues.why: The unsuccessful liquid study makes the sole food-labelled alternative look like the obvious novel comparison.

fairness: Solid-meal provocation is plausible, but rapid-drink challenge can also investigate obstructive physiology. The visible fields lack detailed standard-series metrics or a specific residual hypothesis to establish that competing maneuvers are clinically excluded; 'most directly' narrows the question mainly through stimulus wording.
Importance: esophageal physiologic evaluation is relevant, but selecting a specialist maneuver by food-word matching has modest practical value. Too easy despite technical labels.
Realism: a specialist choosing an added maneuver is plausible; raw manometry findings or an interpretable exhibit are absent.
suggestions: Replace the broad unexplained-series summary with usable, verified manometry observations and the actual residual diagnostic uncertainty.
Compare credible next evaluations whose relative value depends on the findings, without a task that repeats the key's food stimulus.
If no meaningful resident decision remains beyond matching symptoms to the meal, propose consolidation rather than harder terminology.

title: Coverage when the recipient bed cannot support a graft

cues.phrase: will not supply the initial vascular support a skin graft needs
cues.why: Explicitly declares both skin-graft alternatives unsuitable and teaches their dependence on the bed.

cues.phrase: a tissue transfer that retains its feeding vessels
cues.why: Defines the keyed flap mechanism before the options are shown.

cues.phrase: Pedicled tissue-flap coverage
cues.why: The sole flap is a category outlier against two graft variants after the stem has excluded grafts.

fairness: A vascularized flap is the best offered category. The generic recipient-bed description does not identify defect site, size, exposed structures or available pedicle, so the feasibility of this specific coverage plan is not established.
Importance: high reconstructive principle; too easy and not application in its current form.
Realism: a reconstructive consultation fits clinic, but a surface declared unable to support grafts is an author conclusion rather than an operative observation.
suggestions: Describe the actual defect, exposed structures, surrounding tissue and vascular assessment instead of supplying the graft-versus-flap rule.
Compare anatomically feasible coverage options with a real discriminator; verify the proposed pedicled flap is suitable for the stated site.
Use a labelled constructed wound exhibit if visual assessment is the intended objective.

title: Perfusion after a completely detached tissue transfer

cues.phrase: will be detached completely
cues.why: Contradicts preservation of the original donor vascular bridge directly.

cues.phrase: does not leave a connecting tissue bridge
cues.why: Repeats that exclusion in an option-specific negative.

cues.phrase: establishes the transferred tissue's circulation
cues.why: Only the microvascular-anastomosis option supplies a new vascular connection; the other vascular option has already been excluded.

fairness: Microvascular reconnection is the best offered step for the described free tissue transfer. No close procedural alternative is presented.
Importance: a foundational surgery/ABSITE distinction, but low incremental value as a new advanced item. Too easy and one-step.
Realism: discussing a proposed outside reconstruction is plausible; the question tests an operative definition rather than a clinic decision.
suggestions: Seek explicit foundational acceptance or consolidate with the graft/flap item.
For resident application, specify a defect and donor/recipient vascular constraints and ask for a concrete feasible reconstructive plan.
Remove the duplicated bridge negative; do not manufacture difficulty with obscure anastomotic trivia.

title: Operative contamination and a later wound infection

cues.phrase: preserves the timing
cues.why: The task explicitly tells the learner the conceptual rule that separates the original wound class from later infection.

cues.phrase: No inflammation or infection; no respiratory, alimentary, genital or urinary tract entry; asepsis maintained; primary closure
cues.why: The exhibit is nearly a definition of a clean operative wound rather than observations from a specific operation.

cues.phrase: subsequent superficial SSI
cues.why: Identical in every option, so the second purported classification requires no decision and the later-wound exhibit is unnecessary to choosing the key.

fairness: The clean operative class followed by superficial SSI is supported by the stated findings. A subsequent infection does not retrospectively determine the operative contamination class.
Importance: wound classification and SSI documentation are useful, but this is too easy and duplicative of a basic clean-wound definition.
Realism: auditing a wrongly revised record is possible; a named operation and operative findings would be more credible than a checklist of classification criteria.
suggestions: Use a concrete operation and raw contamination findings with a credible adjacent class, rather than a verbatim-style definition.
Ask what specific documentation or prophylaxis-related decision follows at the appropriate time; do not make later SSI identical across all choices if it is meant to be scored.
Remove the preannounced timing rule, while retaining clear chronology.

title: A local contrast event despite an allergy label

cues.phrase: no hives, wheeze, throat symptoms or circulatory change
cues.why: A stacked exclusion list removes the allergic/systemic alternatives without requiring a close differential.

cues.phrase: the current narrative describes a different distribution
cues.why: An interpretive sentence tells the learner to reject the historical generalized-reaction label.

cues.phrase: current injection-site findings
cues.why: The task repeats the local distribution; only the key is local, while both distractors explicitly say 'Generalized' or 'systemic'.

fairness: Extravasation is the best offered explanation for pain and swelling during injection. The stem does not establish extravasation severity or the appropriate disposition.
Importance: high recognition and complication assessment; too easy because the differential is resolved by local-versus-systemic wording.
Realism: reviewing a contrast event and correcting history is plausible. The prior urticarial reaction should remain separately documented; this local event does not negate it.
suggestions: Use actual local progression, skin and neurovascular findings to ask for a concrete management/escalation decision.
Keep necessary systemic observations, but remove the author's 'different distribution' interpretation and compare credible local-complication plans.
Explicitly preserve the separate prior allergic-like history when revising documentation.

title: T-cell suppression does not establish antibody-pathway control

cues.phrase: recipient donor-reactive antibodies in a preimplantation sample
cues.why: Directly supplies 'preformed antibody' rather than requiring inference from timing and findings.

cues.phrase: endothelial binding with complement-associated microvascular thrombosis
cues.why: Almost restates the key's antibody-binding-to-endothelium mechanism.

cues.phrase: Tacrolimus had suppressed T-cell activation
cues.why: Announces that the T-cell pathway was controlled, strongly discouraging the T-cell option.

cues.phrase: despite that tacrolimus effect
cues.why: The task explicitly directs attention away from the mechanism attributed to tacrolimus.

fairness: Preformed antibody-mediated injury is most supported by the described record. Suppressing T-cell activation does not prove all T-cell injury impossible, so the broad wording 'remains compatible' is weaker than asking which mechanism best explains the observed injury.
Importance: transplant immunology is relevant to ABSITE; this is too easy because the mechanism is narrated and then repeated.
Realism: a patient may discuss prior graft injury, but organ, timing and current reason for review are absent. A clinic conversation about a detached mechanism is artificial.
suggestions: Ask which mechanism best explains a concrete graft-injury episode rather than which remains theoretically compatible.
Supply relevant raw timing, immunologic and specimen findings without narrating antibody-endothelium binding as the conclusion.
If testing tacrolimus limitations, link interpretation to a concrete transplant-team assessment decision; do not imply that a reported drug effect excludes all cellular injury.

title: Urgent findings override an elective optimization plan

cues.phrase: acutely painful and cannot be reduced
cues.why: Together with vomiting and guarding, makes the sole emergency-care option obvious; both alternatives remain elective.

cues.phrase: Complete the planned pulmonary optimization course
cues.why: The option openly delays acute assessment for an unrelated prior optimization objective.

cues.phrase: Move the routine elective repair visit forward
cues.why: The 'routine elective' label makes even the nominally accelerated alternative easy to dismiss.

fairness: Emergency surgical evaluation is uniquely appropriate among the offered plans. These red flags are decision-critical and must remain.
Importance: very high safety recognition; clinically important does not mean difficult. Too easy for the requested PGY-2/3 challenge, with no second meaningful step.
Realism: an acute change presenting to clinic is credible. The correct action is transfer/escalation, not clinic management of the obstruction.
suggestions: Retain the red flags and seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety-recognition exception.
If an advanced objective is required, move to a subsequent hospital decision with concrete comparable resuscitation/investigation/operative plans and all necessary observations.
Do not make the initial triage harder by suppressing warning signs or offering unsafe elective delays.

title: Irreversible limb findings and the proposed intervention
fairness: The combination of complete anesthesia/paralysis and absent arterial and venous Doppler signals supports a nonviable-limb interpretation and then a primary-amputation pathway rather than attempted salvage. This is a substantive interpretation-to-action chain.

No reliable nonmedical wording shortcut identified. Although the key says 'assessment' and the others name interventions, amputation is itself a major competing pathway rather than an obviously harmless catch-all.
Importance: very high vascular-surgery/ABSITE decision with a consequential reperfusion-versus-amputation distinction.

Realism: the task explicitly refers to the completed hospital assessment, avoiding an implication that definitive limb treatment occurs in clinic. The retrospective wrapper is somewhat artificial but does not obscure the decision.
Single best offered pathway is defensible on the stated complete findings. Duration alone is not supplied or used as an invented viability threshold. PASS is editorial, not clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional polish: make all three choices parallel hospital pathways, e.g. assessment for primary amputation versus assessment for open or catheter-based revascularization.
Preserve the full sensory, motor and both Doppler findings; reducing them to a generic 'cold pulseless limb' would make the answer unfair.
For future variants, use a supported borderline viability scenario only if the clinician can establish one best action.

title: Reassurance after a negative test

cues.phrase: the cohort's negative-test results
cues.why: Preselects the column before the task repeats the same instruction.

cues.phrase: What proportion of negative tests
cues.why: Supplies the denominator-selection rule explicitly, so the item is table reading rather than interpreting what a negative test means.

cues.phrase: were reference-negative
cues.why: Identifies the numerator directly; the learner needs no diagnostic-test knowledge to select 120/(120+12).

fairness: The arithmetic key is correct: 120 of 132 negative tests are reference-negative. The reference assessment and complete-cohort condition make the computation well-defined.
Importance: predictive values are high-yield evidence literacy, but this exact item is too easy and tests one conditional proportion without clinical application.

Realism: a clinician explaining evidence to a patient is plausible; an unnamed investigational postoperative test with no condition is a generic arithmetic exercise. The disclaimer correctly prevents presenting the constructed cohort as evidence about her care.
suggestions: Keep constructed-data labeling and denominators, but ask for an interpretation or next decision requiring the learner to distinguish cohort NPV from patient-specific reassurance.
Supply a meaningful test/condition context and relevant pretest-risk limitation without inventing clinical thresholds.
If retained as denominator practice, seek explicit basic-item acceptance and remove redundant column-selection prose.

title: Comparing positive-result frequency across reference groups

cues.phrase: how much more often a positive result occurs in those with the condition than in those without it
cues.why: Defines the likelihood-ratio operation in the presentation, reducing the task to dividing the displayed frequencies.

fairness: LR+ is correctly 0.8/0.2 = 4.0. The options are parallel numerical answers, with no key-length or convergence cue.

Equal reference-group totals make dividing the positive counts alone yield the right number; the dataset therefore cannot distinguish correct conditional-rate reasoning from an erroneous raw-count shortcut.
Importance: high-yield diagnostic evidence literacy. Too easy with the definition supplied and symmetric data; two arithmetic operations would not establish two-step clinical reasoning.
Realism: the surgical test and condition are unnamed, so the patient consultation adds no decision relevance.
suggestions: Remove the explanatory definition from the presentation.
Use unequal reference-group sizes so the denominator matters, and use plausible error-derived numerical distractors.

To reach resident application, provide an explicit clinical question and ask how the result changes odds or a subsequent evidence-based action, without treating constructed data as validated clinical evidence.

title: Absolute adverse-event increase and number needed to harm
fairness: The key is mathematically correct: the 30-day excess risk is 0.10 minus 0.05 = 0.05, whose reciprocal is 20. Follow-up period and endpoint are clear.
No exploitable wording, length, grammar, convergence or category cue identified. The difficulty problem is simplicity, not unfair cueing.

Importance: NNH is useful general-surgery/ABSITE evidence literacy, but this is straightforward formula application. Too easy for the requested challenge. Subtracting and taking a reciprocal are arithmetic steps, not two independent clinical inferences.
Realism: dressing counseling fits clinic. A decision about choosing the dressing would also require benefits and relevant patient context, which this narrowly numerical task does not claim to assess.
suggestions: Keep the current exact arithmetic as an explicitly accepted foundational item, or add meaningful benefit/harm data and ask for a justified counseling or choice decision.
For an advanced revision, make the learner compare absolute effects over compatible time horizons rather than merely recall the reciprocal formula.
Do not label the present calculation two-step solely because it uses subtraction followed by inversion.

title: A paired binary change needs a paired analysis

cues.phrase: Patient identities link the two binary observations
cues.why: Supplies the paired-binary classification in nearly the same words as the key.

cues.phrase: paired change
cues.why: The task narrows the answer to paired tests before data interpretation.

cues.phrase: McNemar paired-binary test
cues.why: Only this label matches both adjectives from the presentation; a reader can choose without knowing McNemar's test.

cues.phrase: Fisher independent-group exact test
cues.why: An added explanatory qualifier contradicts 'there is no separate control group' and exposes the distractor's error.

fairness: McNemar is the appropriate offered family for testing paired binary marginal change. The discordant cells make the pairing substantive, though the current task can be answered without reading any table values.
Importance: useful study-design/ABSITE literacy, less frequent in direct clinical care. Too easy because the labels teach the selection rule.
Realism: a wound-care education study is relevant; a patient named solely to host a statistical test-selection exercise is unnecessary clinic framing.
suggestions: Use conventional unannotated test names with comparable specificity, and remove 'paired change' from the lead-in.
Retain the actual repeated-patient design because it is necessary, but let the learner infer binary pairing rather than labeling it.
Make discordant pairs matter to an interpretation or analysis decision, or remove the decorative table if the objective remains study-design recognition.

title: Equivalence requires the prespecified margin comparison

cues.phrase: defines equivalence in mean recovery time as a difference inside -2 to +2 days
cues.why: States the comparison the key repeats; the supplied interval makes that part a simple bounds check.

cues.phrase: within the prespecified two-day bounds
cues.why: Only the key uses the protocol criterion supplied by the stem; both distractors substitute a differently named test.

cues.phrase: requires a significant zero-difference test first
cues.why: Adds an unsupported prerequisite; the other distractor merely restates the nonsignificant-null-test misconception.

fairness: The 90% interval lies inside the stated equivalence margins under the specified TOST protocol, so the keyed conclusion is supported. A nonsignificant superiority/null-difference test is not by itself evidence of equivalence.

The first two options both assert equivalence but offer different reasons. This is closer to selecting an explanation than choosing distinct study conclusions, contrary to the owner's preference for keeping rationale out of options.

Importance: useful evidence interpretation with a real common misconception. Moderate for PGY-2/3 residents less familiar with equivalence methods, but the item requires one supplied-criterion comparison rather than a two-step decision.

Realism: comparing postoperative pathways is relevant; a clinic patient discussing test methodology feels artificial. The teaching-protocol label appropriately avoids claiming that two days is a validated clinical threshold.
suggestions: Present the protocol and interval in a compact constructed exhibit, retaining the prespecified margins and confidence level for fairness.
Offer distinct, parallel conclusions or concrete implementation/research decisions rather than three explanations for equivalence.
Add a genuinely unresolved clinical applicability or endpoint issue if a two-step decision is desired; do not withhold the protocol to make the statistical rule harder.

title: Comparing outcomes at a common surgical case mix
fairness: The key is mathematically supported: each pathway has 10% risk in the straightforward stratum and 40% in the complex stratum; equal standard weights give 25% for each. Crude risks are 13% and 37%, a credible competing calculation.

The learner must distinguish within-stratum risks from the different patient mix, then apply the specified common mix. This supplies a meaningful confounding/standardization problem rather than a second synonymous label.

No exploitable nonmedical option cue identified. Equal weights alone do not imply equal pathway risks; equality follows from interpreting the observed stratum-specific rates. All options use parallel paired percentages.
Importance: moderate-to-high evidence/QI relevance for surgery and ABSITE; avoiding unadjusted comparisons of unlike case mixes is practical.

Realism: an outcomes report fits surgical quality review better than a generic individual clinic conversation, but that wrapper does not alter the calculation. The result is descriptive standardization, not proof of causal equivalence, and the task does not claim otherwise.

Difficulty is an uncalibrated moderate estimate; learners comfortable with weighted averages may find it easy. PASS is editorial and does not establish measured resident performance or clinical approval.
suggestions: Optional improvement: place the same comparison in a surgical outcomes/QI discussion with a concrete proposed interpretation of the crude difference.
Keep the stratum denominators and specified reference weights. Do not replace them with an author conclusion that case mix explains the difference.
If extending to an implementation decision, explicitly distinguish standardized observed risks from causal evidence and retain relevant confounding limitations.
